items.stem: What is the most effective way to reduce PCI DSS scope?

options.text: Segment and avoid storing cardholder data wherever possible
options.rationale: Correct: fewer systems touching card data means less scope.

options.text: Store all card data in one big database
options.rationale: Centralising storage increases, not reduces, scope and risk.

options.text: Use default device passwords for consistency
options.rationale: Default passwords are a classic weakness, not a scope reducer.
Logging is required; disabling it is non-compliant.

items.explanation: Correct: segmentation and not storing card data reduce scope.

items.stem: Which TWO are common PCI DSS compliance pitfalls? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Leaving vendor default passwords in place
options.rationale: Correct: default credentials are a frequent and serious gap.
Correct: gaps in patching and logging are common failures.
Segmentation is good practice, not a pitfall.
Minimising stored data reduces risk; it is not a pitfall.

items.explanation: Correct: default passwords and inconsistent patching/logging are common pitfalls.

items.stem: Why is storing sensitive authentication data after authorisation discouraged?

options.text: It is high-value to attackers and generally must not be retained
options.rationale: Correct: such data should not be stored after authorisation.
Storing it does not speed transactions and adds risk.

options.text: It is required for every refund
options.rationale: Refunds do not require retaining prohibited authentication data.

options.text: It reduces the systems in scope
options.rationale: Storing more sensitive data increases scope and risk.

items.explanation: Correct: sensitive authentication data should not be retained after authorisation.
